title: Inhaled biologics: A paradigm shift in drug delivery for proteins, vaccines, and gene-based therapeutics.

abstract: The advancement of RNA therapeutics, particularly small interfering RNA (siRNA), offers promising new approaches for the treatment of pulmonary diseases driven by aberrant gene expression and chronic inflammation like asthma and COPD. In this study, we systematically engineered dry powder inhaler (DPI) formulations containing low (0.8%) and high (2%) siRNA-loaded lipid nanoparticle (LNP) concentrations using spray drying. The matrix-forming excipients, lactose, mannitol and trehalose were combined with varying concentrations of L-leucine (3% to 30% relative to the sugar or sugar alcohol) and trileucine (3%) as dispersion enhancers. The goal was to address key formulation hurdles: maintaining siRNA gene-silencing efficiency, optimizing solid-state properties, and achieving efficient aerosolization for pulmonary delivery. Lactose and trehalose-based spray-dried powders exhibited yields over 70% and preserved siRNA bioactivity, with gene silencing efficiencies exceeding 95% in vitro. Physicochemical characterization revealed that these formulations containing low to moderate leucine or trileucine content solidified in the glassy state, displaying glass transition temperatures over 76 °C and residual moisture levels below 7%, favorable for long-term stability and pulmonary delivery. In contrast, mannitol-based formulations were highly crystalline and less compatible with LNPs, resulting in low yields, larger, irregular shaped particles and poor aerosolization efficiency. In vitro aerosol performance was assessed using two breath-actuated DPIs in a laser diffraction inhalation setup. Our findings highlight that successful pulmonary delivery of siRNA-LNP powders not only depend on powder attributes but also on the interplay between formulation and DPI device. Optimizing excipient selection with regard to a device's powder dispersion principle is essential to achieve robust aerosol performance, efficient lung deposition, and preservation of therapeutic activity in solid-state siRNA-LNP dry powder formulations.

title: Systematic excipient selection as a tool to optimize solid state properties and aerosol performance of spray dried RNA loaded lipid nanoparticles.

abstract: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a fatal neurodegenerative disease characterized by progressive motor neuron loss. Aberrant RNA metabolism is one of its most consistent molecular features, and ALS has long been framed as a disease of RNA-binding proteins (RBPs), given that mutations in RBPs are among the most frequent genetic causes of ALS. However, a growing number of ALS-associated genes encode proteins that lack canonical RNA-binding domains; nonetheless, their mutations also disrupt RNA homeostasis. This review examines how these non-canonical disease modulators perturb RNA metabolism. We group these factors into three functional classes. One includes proteostasis regulators, whose dysfunction impairs protein quality control and promotes the accumulation of aggregation-prone RBPs in cytoplasmic inclusions and persistent stress granules. Another involves factors that elicit RNA toxicity or disrupt ribonucleoprotein organization, including GGGGCC repeat expansion in C9ORF72 and CAG repeat expansion in ATXN1. The third class comprises factors governing axonal RNA granule transport. Across these categories, a shared consequence is the disruption of mRNA processing, stability, localization, and translation in motor neurons. We further discuss how epitranscriptomic dysregulation, particularly altered m6A and m1A modification states, may contribute to ALS pathology. We also discuss the therapeutic implications of this mechanistic convergence in defective RNA metabolism in ALS.

title: All Roads Lead to Rome: Non-canonical Modulators of RNA Metabolism in ALS Pathogenesis.

abstract: Pigs and chickens are not only the most important livestock species for global food production but also serve as key model organisms in various research disciplines. The pig is widely used in translational research due to its anatomical and physiological similarity to humans, providing valuable insights into immunology, metabolism, and disease mechanisms. In contrast, the chicken has become an essential model for studies related to poultry health, animal welfare, and developmental biology. Its externally developing embryo offers exceptional accessibility for experimental manipulation. Recent advances in genome editing technologies, particularly CRISPR/Cas9, have further expanded the potential of these species for functional genomic studies, although the efficient delivery of such tools remains a major challenge. Here, we overcome this delivery limitation by using virus-like particles (VLPs). We evaluated VLPs as delivery vehicles for genome engineering tools in porcine and avian cultures, two key livestock species at the human-animal interface. VLP-mediated delivery enabled efficient Cre recombination and high CRISPR/Cas9 editing rates in porcine cells, organoids, and oocytes, particularly when multiplexed. In chickens, VLPs supported robust Cre recombination and Cas9-mediated editing in cell culture, tracheal organ cultures, and in ovo. Reporter VLPs and dCas9 VLPs further demonstrated the versatility of this platform across porcine and avian systems. Together, these findings establish VLPs as an efficient and time-saving strategy for gene editing in livestock cultures across in vitro, ex vivo and in ovo systems, with potential future applications for animal health, agricultural productivity, and translational One Health research.

title: Virus-like particles enable highly efficient gene editing across porcine and avian in vitro, ex vivo, and in ovo models.

abstract: Human papillomavirus (HPV) infection and related cancers remain significant public health concerns worldwide. Among high-risk HPV genotypes, HPV16 demonstrates the highest epidemiological prevalence. The viral oncoproteins E6 and E7 are crucial drivers of HPV16-associated carcinogenesis and have become key therapeutic targets for treating HPV16-related cervical intraepithelial neoplasia and cancers. HPV prophylactic vaccines have been widely implemented in clinical practice; however, effective therapeutic interventions for infected individuals remain limited. Therefore, the development of therapeutic HPV vaccines is urgently needed. LY01620 is an investigational mRNA therapeutic vaccine targeting HPV16 E6/E7 antigens. To support LY01620's clinical trial application and development, comprehensive nonclinical studies were conducted, including immunogenicity evaluations in mice and rats, anti-tumor activity and mechanistic studies in C3.43 tumor-bearing mice, single-dose tissue distribution study in rats, and a GLP-compliant repeated-dose toxicity study in rats combined with toxicokinetics, local irritation, and immunotoxicity assessments. LY01620 demonstrated strong immunogenicity in mice and rats and exhibited significant anti-tumor activity through inducing a strong Th1-polarized immune response, increasing frequency of antigen-specific T cells, and enhancing infiltration of CD8+ T cells and mature macrophages into tumors. LY01620 mRNA exhibited sustained accumulation in inguinal lymph nodes and spleens, potentially facilitating persistent antigen presentation and prolonged immunological effects. In the repeated-dose toxicity study in SD rats, LY01620 exhibited a favorable safety profile, with the no observed adverse effect level was the highest dose of 300 μg/animal. In conclusion, preclinical studies have demonstrated that LY01620 exhibited favorable mechanism of action-related efficacy and a well-tolerated safety profile, supporting its further development.

title: Nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology studies of LY01620, a therapeutic mRNA vaccine against human papillomavirus 16-related cancers.

abstract: While clinical translation of messenger RNA (mRNA) lipid nanoparticle (LNP) technologies has redefined vaccinology, the development of potent platforms against complex bacterial pathogens is often limited by the transient expression kinetics and rapid clearance of encoded antigens. One well established approach to enhance immunogenicity is the fusion of an Fc fragment to an antigen. However, the mechanism of Fc-mediated potentiation within mRNA-LNP systems is, yet, undefined, specifically regarding the necessity of receptor-mediated interactions. Here, we demonstrate that an mRNA-LNP vaccine, encoding an Fc-fragment fused to the Yersinia pestis F1 antigen, drives robust, protective immunity against the lethal bubonic plague by functioning as a pharmacokinetic stabilizer. Through systematic architectural design, variation of Fc isotypes, species-matched scaffolding, and glycosylation profiling, we reveal that Fc-integration extends systemic antigen bioavailability by over 300-fold, providing a sustained kinetic window for immune priming. Remarkably, immunogenicity is preserved in Fcγ receptor (FcγR)-deficient mice, as well as with a reduced FcγR-binding Fc variant, suggesting that protective immunity is independent of classical FcγR engagement in this model. These findings decouple Fc-mediated enhancement from receptor-mediated interactions, identifying structural stabilization and prolonged persistence as the primary drivers of efficacy in mRNA-LNP vaccines. Altogether, our results provide a mechanistic framework for the design of high-potency mRNA vaccines through engineered protein stability.

title: mRNA-LNP vaccine encoding for Fc-scaffold antigen drives FcγR-independent immunity.

abstract: RNA molecules adopt diverse secondary structures for distinct functions. Among them, the left-handed RNA double helix (Z-RNA) regulates innate immunity and has been implicated in autoimmune disorders. However, accurate, fine-scale Z-RNome profiling remain lacking, and its role in autoimmune diseases like systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is poorly understood. Here we develop AMAZE-seq for fine-scale profiling of the human Z-RNome. AMAZE-seq leverages the Zα domain for specific recognition of Z-RNA and a fused APOBEC1 enzyme to edit Z-RNA regions for subsequent detection. Using AMAZE-seq, we reveal that Z-RNAs predominantly form on intramolecular double-stranded RNA rich in pyrimidine/purine alternations, with nearly half originating from non-repetitive regions, substantially expanding the known repertoire of Z-RNA-forming regions. Knockout and rescue experiments support the role of ADAR1 p150 in suppressing Z-RNA through both binding and RNA editing. AMAZE-seq profiling of SLE patient-derived cells reveals a dysregulated Z-RNome. Mechanistically, elevated Z-RNA formation activates ZBP1 and induces RIPK3-MLKL-mediated necroptosis and caspase-dependent apoptosis, potentially triggering the release of immunogenic Z-RNA species and aberrant immune responses in SLE patients. Our results define the landscape, features, regulatory mechanisms, and disease relevance of Z-RNA, establishing AMAZE-seq as a transformative tool for dissecting Z-RNA biology in health and disease.

title: Z-RNome profiling uncovers dysregulated Z-RNA with implications in systemic lupus erythematosus pathogenesis.

abstract: The Hippo-YAP/TEAD signaling axis regulates tissue growth, cellular identity, and organ homeostasis. Dysregulation of this pathway, through NF2 loss, LATS1 or LATS2 inactivation, or YAP1- or WWTR1-derived gene fusions, results in persistent nuclear localization of YAP/TAZ, driving TEAD-dependent transcriptional programs. NF2-deficient and YAP1/TAZ-driven tumors, such as mesothelioma, schwannoma, meningioma, and epithelioid hemangioendothelioma, exemplify Hippo-pathway dependency and are potential therapeutic targets. Targeting TEAD disrupts transcriptional circuits sustaining tumor growth, plasticity, and immune suppression while modulating metabolic and stromal dependencies. Pharmacologic interventions targeting YAP/TEAD include TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors, direct YAP/TEAD protein-protein interaction disruptors, PROTAC-mediated TEAD degraders, and YAP-directed antisense oligonucleotide strategies. Early-phase trials have demonstrated preliminary clinical activity, particularly with TEAD palmitate-binding pocket inhibitors in mesothelioma and have been associated with mild drug-related toxicities, such as proteinuria. YAP/TEAD inhibition may also be a rational combinatorial approach given the emergence of adaptive resistance mechanisms to EGFR/KRAS inhibitors and immunotherapies. Collectively, these findings provide rationale and early proof-of-concept for the pharmacologic targeting of the YAP/TEAD pathway. In this review, we describe the biological underpinnings of the YAP/TEAD pathway in cancer medicine, the anti-cancer strategies targeting this pathway, and discuss future directions in the field.

title: Emerging strategies targeting the Hippo-YAP/TEAD pathway and the translational relevance in solid tumors.

abstract: RNA-lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) are emerging tools for poultry vaccination, but methods for local protein expression in reproductive tissues remain underdeveloped. Here, we established RNA delivery to chicken testes using LNPs formulated with the ionizable lipid DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3) and multifocal intratesticular injection through an intercostal surgical approach. Bilateral injections were completed in all six chickens in a surgical-feasibility cohort, with postoperative recovery during the 7-day observation period. At an equal RNA mass dose of 80 µg per testis, conventional messenger RNA (mRNA) encoding enhanced green fluorescent protein (eGFP) produced detectable reporter signals at days 1, 3, and 7, with the highest measured signal at day 3. An eGFP self-amplifying RNA (saRNA) construct showed delayed detectable expression at days 3 and 7. Delivery of mRNAs encoding CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) and the epitope-tagged recombination-related proteins DNA meiotic recombinase 1 (DMC1) and RAD51 recombinase (RAD51) also produced detectable proteins in testicular tissue. Following local delivery, testicular architecture was preserved, with minimal apoptosis and only a modest inflammatory response. These findings establish the feasibility of local RNA-LNP delivery for short-term protein production in chicken testes, providing a platform for future studies of male reproduction and genome editing.

title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNA delivery enables protein expression in chicken testes.

abstract: Lassa virus (LASV) causes severe hemorrhagic fever across West Africa, yet no licensed vaccine is available. A major barrier to LASV antigen design is that its sole neutralization target, the glycoprotein complex (GPC), lacks intrinsic late-domain motifs required to engage the host ESCRT machinery for particle release. Here, we report a rational design strategy that confers autonomous budding capacity to LASV GPC by appending a synthetic ESCRT-recruitment cassette to its cytoplasmic domain. Systematic screening of a sixteen-construct matrix identified a lead candidate, VLPdEm5. This construct integrates the ESCRT cassette, an optimized furin cleavage site, and a heterologous H1N1 transmembrane-cytoplasmic domain to support efficient particle assembly and proper display of conformational neutralizing epitopes. Delivered via lipid-nanoparticle-encapsulated mRNA (mRNA-LNP), VLPdEm5 drives efficient in situ virus-like particle (VLP) self-assembly, eliciting rapid, high-titer binding antibodies with broad cross-reactivity across six major LASV lineages, robust germinal center B-cell activity, and memory T-cell responses. Crucially, VLPdEm5 mRNA-LNP provides dose-dependent protection against pseudovirus challenge in vivo. This work establishes an effective LASV vaccine candidate and validates an ESCRT-engineered mRNA-VLP platform broadly applicable to non-budding viral envelope proteins.

abstract:
SHIPSS is a multi-institutional, prospective, controlled, randomized, double-blinded interventional trial that will examine the potential benefits and risks of adjunctive hydrocortisone prescribed for children with fluid and vasoactive-inotropic refractory septic shock.

It is hypothesized that adjunctive hydrocortisone will significantly reduce the incidence of new and progressive organ dysfunction (primary outcome) and proportion of children with poor outcomes, defined as death or severely impaired health-related quality of life (HRQL) (secondary outcome), as assessed at 28 days following study enrollment (randomization).

description:
Sepsis represents the most common cause of childhood mortality worldwide. In the United States alone, 200 cases of pediatric sepsis are diagnosed each day, with an associated hospital mortality rate of 5-10% and health care expenditures now approaching $5 billion annually. Moreover, nearly one third of children admitted to pediatric intensive care units (PICUs) for septic shock have not regained their baseline health-related quality of life one year following the sepsis event.

During early resuscitation of the child with septic shock, in addition to antibiotics, volume replacement, and vasoactive-inotropic support, the most recent pediatric treatment guidelines advise the practitioner to consider adjunctive hydrocortisone therapy if the patient "is at risk of absolute adrenal insufficiency or adrenal pituitary axis failure". However, the potential benefits and risks of this recommendation have not been rigorously examined. On the one hand, corticosteroids are inexpensive and have been frequently demonstrated to improve hemodynamic status in children and adults with sepsis. Conversely, this drug class is known to alter transcription of approximately 30% of the human genome. Notably, corticosteroids down regulate most aspects of the immune response, but particularly adaptive immunity. Moreover, recent data suggests that children with particular gene expression profiles in sepsis have increased likelihood of mortality when treated with corticosteroids.

SHIPSS (Stress Hydrocortisone In Pediatric Septic Shock) is a prospective, randomized, double-blinded, placebo-controlled trial examining the potential benefits and risks of adjunctive hydrocortisone prescribed to critically ill children with fluid and vasoactive-inotropic refractory septic shock. Up to 500 children will be enrolled, randomized, and evaluated at baseline, and 28 and 90 days following study enrollment.

The primary hypothesis is that hydrocortisone, compared to placebo, will decrease the the incidence of new or progressive organ dysfunction (primary outcome) and the proportion of subjects with poor outcomes, defined as death or severely impaired (≥25% decrease from baseline) HRQL (secondary outcome). Subjects will be monitored daily while receiving care in the PICU for the occurrence of adverse events, including the following protocol specified events:hyperglycemia treated with any insulin; gastrointestinal hemorrhage treated with blood product transfusion or vasopressin or octreotide infusion; delirium requiring medical treatment; and hospital-acquired infection treated with new antimicrobials. Finally, the investigators will test the hypothesis that biomarker-based prognostic and predictive enrichment strategies can improve our ability to identify which children with septic shock are more likely to benefit from adjunctive hydrocortisone, and which may be harmed. This trial will have a significant impact on public health by providing the heretofore missing evidence to inform guidelines regarding therapy for septic shock in children.

The SHIPSS trial will enroll patients from PICUs in Canada, the United States, Saudi Arabia, Israel, Brazil, Vietnam, Pakistan, Japan, Malaysia, and Singapore. Health Canada approval is not required as hydrocortisone is approved for use in septic shock in children, and this trial meets the criteria of a Phase IV study. In the United States, this trial is considered a Phase III trial as hydrocortisone is not approved for use in pediatric septic shock.

outcomes.description: Appearance of new or progression of existing organ dysfunctions according to PELOD-2 definitions. PELOD-2 considers 5 organ dysfunctions (neurological, cardiovascular, renal, respiratory, and hematological) with 10 total variables, with dysfunction scored 0 up to 6 for each organ category. Total minimum/maximal scores are 0/33, with increasing score indicating increasing risk of mortality. Logit (mortality) = -6.61 + 0.47 × PELOD-2 score. Probability of death = 1/(1 + exp \[-logit(mortality)\]). A new organ dysfunction or progression of organ dysfunction is defined as an increase score in any organ category from baseline.
outcomes.measure: New or progressive multiple organ dysfunction syndrome as assessed utilizing the Pediatric Logistic Organ Dysfunction (PELOD-2) instrument.

outcomes.description: Mortality or ≥25% decrease in PedsQL from baseline
outcomes.measure: 28-day hospital mortality or ≥25% decrease from baseline in health-related quality of life (HRQL) assessed utilizing the Pediatric Quality of Life Inventory, (PedsQL)

outcomes.description: Occurrence of adverse events plausibly associated with corticosteroid administration. SHIPSS specified events include hyperglycemia, gastrointestinal hemorrhage, delirium, and hospital-acquired infection
outcomes.measure: SHIPSS specified adverse events

outcomes.description: Risk stratification sepsis biomarkers will be measured in serum obtained at enrollment and on Day 2. The PERSEVERE (PEdiatRic SEpsis biomarkEr Risk modEl) will be used to determine the patient's risk of mortality. mRNA will be isolated from blood samples collected at enrollment and on Day 2 to classify the patient as pediatric septic shock Endotype B or A. A composite outcome of sepsis endotype and PERSEVERE risk of mortality will be used to determine if a biomarker-based prognostic model and predictive enrichment strategies allow identification of children with septic shock more likely to benefit from adjunctive hydrocortisone. We hypothesize that pediatric septic shock "endotype B" subjects having an intermediate to high Pediatric Sepsis Biomarker Risk Model (PERSEVERE)-based risk of mortality will derive significant benefit from adjunctive corticosteroids, compared to endotype B subjects having a low risk and endotype A subjects at all risk levels.
outcomes.measure: Risk stratification sepsis biomarkers and pediatric sepsis endotype

outcomes.description: This is a 3-level ordinal endpoint, with levels death, survival with severely impaired HRQL (≥25% decrease from baseline), and survival without severely impaired HRQL, assessed at 28 and 90 days. This approach is similar to that recently reported for assessment of functional status among children encountering critical illness, utilizing the Functional Status Scale. This endpoint is expected to be highly correlated with the primary efficacy endpoint.
outcomes.measure: Trichotomous mortality/morbidity outcome

outcomes.description: Mortality or ≥25% decrease in PedsQL from baseline
outcomes.measure: 90-Day Death or ≥25% decrease in HRQL from baseline

outcomes.measure: Vasoactive-inotropic infusion-free days through day 28

outcomes.description: Mechanical ventilation-free days through day 28 is defined as 28 minus duration of mechanical ventilation. Subjects who die, are still receiving mechanical ventilation, or are transferred from the PICU still receiving mechanical ventilation by day 28 will be censored at 28 days and assigned zero mechanical ventilation-free days.
outcomes.measure: Mechanical ventilation-free days through day 28

outcomes.description: Proportion of subjects receiving acute RRT. All types of acute RRT will be considered, including hemodialysis, continuous venovenous hemofiltration (CVVH), continuous venovenous hemodialysis (CVVHD), and peritoneal dialysis. RRT in patients on chronic RRT will not be considered.
outcomes.measure: Utilization of acute renal replacement therapy (RRT)
outcomes.time_frame: Enrollment to PICU discharge, an average of 2 weeks

outcomes.measure: Functional status - FSS

outcomes.measure: PICU-free days through day 28

outcomes.description: Hospital-free days through day 28 is defined as 28 minus duration of hospital stay. Subjects who die or are still in the hospital by day 28 will be censored at 28 days and assigned zero hospital-free days through day 28.
outcomes.measure: Hospital-free days through day 28

abstract: Helminth infections affect over 1.5 billion people and weaken the response to vaccination. CORBEVAX contains the TLR9-activating adjuvant CpG 1018, which may overcome this. This trial measures the immunogenicity of CORBEVAX in adults with and without Schistosoma mansoni or hookworm infection in Ethiopia. The primary measure is spike-specific serum IgG at Day 42; antibody subclass, T-cell, neutralisation and regulatory T-cell responses are measured as secondary outcomes up to Day 90. This is the first of two planned cohorts under a shared protocol; a second cohort receiving an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine at the same sites is planned subject to vaccine availability and will be registered separately.

description:
Adults aged 18 years or older living in helminth -endemic (Schistosoma mansoni and hookworm ) areas of Ethiopia (Bahir Dar and Arba Minch) are recruited by community-based mobilisation, screened by parasitological examination (direct wet mount and Kato-Katz) and classified as helminth-infected or uninfected before enrolment. The study has a single arm: every participant receives CORBEVAX intramuscularly (0.5 ml undiluted) at Day 0 with a homologous booster at Day 28, and the helminth-infected and uninfected groups differ by baseline exposure rather than by assigned intervention. Serum is collected at Day 0, Day 42 and Day 90, and peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMC) are isolated at Day 0 and Day 42, so that all cell-based outcomes have a pre-vaccination baseline. Infected participants receive anthelminthic treatment after the Day 42 blood draw. Immunological assays are run at Aarhus University, with neutralizing antibody testing at Biological E, India.

This study is the first of two sequential cohorts conducted under a shared protocol, at the same study sites, with the same field teams, eligibility criteria, visit schedule, outcome measures and laboratory assays. A second cohort, in which participants will receive an mRNA COVID-19 vaccine (BNT162b2, or mRNA-1273 if BNT162b2 cannot be obtained), is planned to begin enrolment approximately one month after the last participant is enrolled in the present cohort, subject to vaccine availability, and will be registered as a separate record carrying the same protocol identifier.

Participants are not allocated to a vaccine platform: the vaccine a participant receives is determined by which cohort is enrolling at the time. Because each cohort contains its own contemporaneous helminth-uninfected comparison group, a prespecified secondary analysis will compare the infected-versus-uninfected response ratio between the two cohorts (a difference-in-differences comparison across vaccine platforms) rather than comparing vaccine groups directly. Serum and PBMC samples from both cohorts will be stored and assayed together in a single batch with shared reference standards and bridging controls, and baseline anti-nucleocapsid serology will be measured in both cohorts to document comparability of prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure. Antigen, dose and formulation differ between the two vaccine platforms, so any between-cohort difference cannot be attributed to adjuvants alone.

A single primary outcome is specified: spike-specific serum IgG concentration at Day 42. Serum is obtained from every participant at every visit and the assay is performed in-house, so this measure is the one least exposed to sample or logistical failure. All remaining immunological read-outs are secondary. Analyses that require viable PBMC will be performed in every participant from whom cells of adequate viability are recovered; if adequate cells are not recovered in a sufficient proportion of participants, those analyses will be reported as exploratory rather than omitted. Serum, PBMC and faecal aliquots are biobanked under the storage consent, so any assay deferred for sample or budget reasons can be completed later rather than lost.

outcomes.description: Concentration of IgG binding the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein in serum, measured by in-house enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and expressed in arbitrary units per mL (AU/mL). Reported as the geometric mean concentration with 95% confidence interval, separately for participants with and without helminth infection (Kato-Katz positive vs negative at Day 0). Day 42 is 14 days after the second vaccine dose.
outcomes.measure: Geometric mean concentration of serum anti-SARS-CoV-2 spike IgG, by helminth infection status

outcomes.description: Concentration of serum IgG binding the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, measured by in-house ELISA (AU/mL). Reported as the geometric mean concentration with 95% confidence interval at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Geometric mean concentration of serum anti-spike IgG at Day 0 and Day 90, by helminth infection status

outcomes.description: Concentration of serum IgG binding the receptor-binding domain (RBD) of the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, measured by in-house ELISA (AU/mL). Reported as the geometric mean concentration with 95% confidence interval at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: RBD-specific binding antibody concentration (serum IgG)

outcomes.description: Concentration of serum IgG binding the SARS-CoV-2 nucleocapsid protein, measured by in-house ELISA and expressed in arbitrary units per mL (AU/mL). Anti-nucleocapsid IgG documents prior SARS-CoV-2 exposure, because nucleocapsid is not part of the vaccine, and supports comparability with the planned mRNA cohort. Reported as the geometric mean concentration with 95% confidence interval at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Nucleocapsid-specific binding antibody concentration (serum IgG)

outcomes.description: Concentration of spike-specific IgG1, IgG2, IgG3 and IgG4 in serum, each measured by in-house subclass-specific ELISA and expressed in arbitrary units per mL (AU/mL). Each subclass is reported separately as the geometric mean concentration with 95% confidence interval at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Concentration of spike-specific IgG subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3 and IgG4) in serum

outcomes.description: Ratio of spike-specific IgG4 to spike-specific IgG1 concentration for each participant, both measured by in-house subclass-specific ELISA (AU/mL) and expressed as a unitless ratio. Reported as the geometric mean ratio with 95% confidence interval at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Ratio of spike-specific IgG4 to spike-specific IgG1 concentration in serum

outcomes.description: Capacity of serum to neutralise SARS-CoV-2, measured by pseudovirus neutralisation assay on serial serum dilutions. Reported as NT50, the reciprocal serum dilution giving 50% reduction in infection (titre units), as the geometric mean titre with 95% confidence interval, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Serum SARS-CoV-2 50% neutralising antibody titre (NT50)

outcomes.description: Percentage of CD4+ T cells in PBMC expressing each of three lineage-defining transcription factors: T-BET (Th1), GATA3 (Th2) and RORγt (Th17). Each factor is measured by intranuclear staining and flow cytometry, expressed as % of CD4+ T cells, and reported separately, to assess helminth-related skewing of T cell phenotype.
outcomes.measure: Percentage of CD4+ T cells expressing the transcription factors T-BET, GATA3 and RORγt

outcomes.description: Percentage of CD4+CD25+FoxP3+ regulatory T cells among total CD4+ T cells in PBMC, measured by flow cytometry with surface and intranuclear staining (% of CD4+ T cells). Reported as the median with interquartile range, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Percentage of regulatory T cells among CD4+ T cells

outcomes.description: Percentage of CD4+ T cells and, separately, CD8+ T cells in PBMC that produce IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, granzyme B or IL-10, or express the activation marker CD154, after stimulation with SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide pools. Each marker is measured by intracellular cytokine staining and flow cytometry and reported separately as % of the parent T-cell population after subtracting the unstimulated control.
outcomes.measure: Percentage of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells producing or expressing IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, granzyme B, IL-10 or CD154 after SARS-CoV-2 spike peptide stimulation

outcomes.description: Concentration of Th1-associated (IFN-γ, TNF-α, IL-2, CXCL10) and Th2-associated (IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, CCL17) cytokines and chemokines in serum, each measured by multiplex bead-based immunoassay and expressed in pg/mL. Each analyte is reported separately as the median with interquartile range at each time point, by helminth infection status.
outcomes.measure: Serum cytokine and chemokine concentrations

outcomes.description: Number of helminth eggs per gram of stool (EPG), measured by Kato-Katz thick smear microscopy. EPG is the mean egg count from two thick smears prepared from a single stool sample, multiplied by 24 (41.7 mg template). Reported separately for Schistosoma mansoni and hookworm as the geometric mean EPG with 95% confidence interval.
outcomes.measure: Helminth infection intensity (eggs per gram of stool), by species

outcomes.description: Percentage of participants with EPG = 0 on Kato-Katz microscopy at Day 90 among participants with EPG \> 0 at baseline, assessed separately for Schistosoma mansoni and hookworm, following anthelmintic treatment given after Day 42. Newly acquired infection (EPG \> 0 at Day 90 among participants with EPG = 0 at baseline) will be addressed in a prespecified sensitivity analysis.
outcomes.measure: Percentage of participants with parasitological clearance

outcomes.description: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rho) between two measures in the same participants: (1) baseline EPG, measured by Kato-Katz thick smear at Day 0 (eggs per gram of stool); and (2) serum anti-spike IgG concentration at Day 42, measured by in-house ELISA (AU/mL). Calculated separately for Schistosoma mansoni and hookworm. Reported with 95% confidence interval.
outcomes.measure: Correlation between baseline helminth egg count and Day 42 anti-spike IgG concentration

outcomes.description: Spearman's rank correlation coefficient (rho) between two measures in the same participants: (1) baseline faecal bacterial alpha diversity, expressed as the Shannon index (unitless), calculated from 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing (V3-V4 region) of a single stool sample collected at Day 0; and (2) serum anti-spike IgG concentration at Day 42, measured by in-house ELISA and expressed in arbitrary units per mL (AU/mL). Reported with 95% confidence interval.
outcomes.measure: Correlation between baseline gut microbiota alpha diversity and Day 42 serum anti-spike IgG concentration

outcomes.description: Number and percentage of participants reporting at least one solicited local or systemic adverse event (injection-site pain, redness or swelling, fatigue, headache, fever, myalgia) or any unsolicited adverse event, including serious adverse events, after each vaccine dose.
outcomes.measure: Number and percentage of participants with solicited and unsolicited adverse events after vaccination

abstract: Protozoan parasites possess complex genomes, unusual DNA-repair mechanisms, multiple developmental stages, and, in several species, intracellular or vector-dependent life cycles that complicate functional genetic studies. CRISPR-Cas9 has become a central tool for functional genomics in these organisms, enabling targeted gene disruption, replacement, tagging, nucleotide modification and genome-wide functional screening. However, editing efficiency and outcomes vary substantially among parasite species and depend not only on Cas9-mediated double-strand break formation but also on target accessibility, guide design, delivery method, parasite stage, DNA-repair capacity, donor availability, selection and the biological cost of the induced lesion. This review focuses primarily on experimentally established Cas9-mediated genome editing in Plasmodium, Leishmania, Toxoplasma gondii, Trypanosoma, Babesia, Theileria and Cryptosporidium. We compare plasmid-based and transient expression, ribonucleoprotein (RNP) delivery, electroporation/nucleofection, stage-specific delivery, guide and donor design, selection strategies, editing outcomes, and molecular and functional validation. Particular emphasis is placed on homology-directed repair (HDR), canonical non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), microhomology-mediated end joining (MMEJ) and single-strand annealing (SSA), which determine whether editing results in indels, precise sequence replacement, tagging or larger genomic deletions. Species-specific differences are illustrated by efficient NHEJ-mediated disruption in Toxoplasma, donor-dependent repair in Plasmodium and Cryptosporidium, SSA-associated repair in Leishmania, efficient homologous recombination in trypanosomatids, precise editing in Babesia, and stage-specific delivery constraints in Theileria. The review further examines the progression from single-gene editing to marker-free manipulation, base editing, conditional approaches and genome-wide functional screens. Cas12a, CRISPRi/a, prime editing and related systems are discussed as emerging extensions. Overall, this repair- and delivery-centred framework explains why CRISPR editing differs among protozoan parasites and identifies the experimentally validated limitations that currently shape their genome-engineering potential.

title: CRISPR-Cas Systems in Protozoan Parasites: Genome Editing, Functional Genomics, Gene Regulation and Emerging Applications.

abstract: Rapid and sensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus (S. aureus) is critical for food safety and public health. Herein, this work developed an ABC (aptamer-B-PER-CRISPR) cascade detection platform, where B-PER stands for bidirectional primer exchange reaction, that integrates aptamer-mediated target recognition, B-PER isothermal amplification, and CRISPR/Cas12a trans-cleavage for highly sensitive and specific detection of S. aureus. Upon target recognition, the trigger strand T is released from the aptamer-T duplex, initiating B-PER to generate abundant products containing sequences recognized by the guide RNA (gRNA), which activate Cas12a to cleave the reporter probe, generating a detectable fluorescence signal. Under optimized conditions, the platform exhibited a linear range of 102 to 1010 CFU per mL with a regression equation of F520 nm = 575.36 log C + 3246.47 (R2 = 0.9992) and a limit of detection of 13 CFU per mL. The assay showed excellent specificity for S. aureus, with negligible cross-reactivity toward Vibrio parahaemolyticus and Salmonella. Recovery tests in spiked milk samples yielded average recoveries of 98.9-100.7%. Overall, the ABC platform offers high sensitivity, excellent specificity, robust anti-interference capability, and operational simplicity, demonstrating great potential for rapid and reliable detection of foodborne pathogens in complex matrices.

title: A programmable aptamer-triggered B-PER/CRISPR cascade amplification platform for ultrasensitive detection of Staphylococcus aureus.

abstract: RNA editing, a post-transcriptional process altering RNA sequences, is crucial in cancer progression. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) editing, mediated by ADAR enzymes, and cytosine-to-uridine (C-to-U) editing, by APOBEC proteins, diversify the transcriptome and proteome. Dysregulation of RNA editing significantly impacts gene expression, promoting tumorigenesis through alterations in amino acid sequences, transcript stability, and miRNA targeting. Conflicting research highlights the complexity of RNA editing's role in cancer. While hyper-editing often correlates with editase overexpression and aggressive phenotypes, hypo-editing links to lower expression. Specific RNA editing events, rather than overall levels, offer more precise insights. ADAR1 primarily promotes oncogenesis, while ADAR2 generally acts as a tumor suppressor. ADAR3's role remains unclear. RNA editing also influences noncoding RNAs, including miRNAs and lncRNAs, affecting their function and stability. A-to-I editing regulates miRNA biogenesis and mRNA-miRNA interactions, altering target gene selection and processing. LncRNAs, susceptible to A-to-I editing, undergo modifications that disrupt crucial molecular interactions, impacting their roles as miRNA sponges and regulators of gene expression. CircRNAs, through ADAR-mediated regulation, contribute to the complexity of RNA editing's influence on cancer. This review underscores RNA editing's multifaceted role in cancer, impacting key signaling pathways and immune surveillance. Understanding these mechanisms is vital for developing targeted therapies and improving cancer outcomes.

title: The multifaceted role of a-to-i rna editing in tumorigenesis: from coding to noncoding RNAs.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas12a is widely used for genome editing because it is simple, efficient, and suitable for multiplex targeting. However, strong or prolonged Cas12a activity can increase unwanted cleavage at off-target sites. This problem is especially important when Cas12a is used in complex microbial communities, where unintended editing may affect non-target microorganisms or mobile genetic elements. Anti-CRISPR (Acr) proteins are natural inhibitors of CRISPR-Cas systems. Acr proteins targeting type V-A CRISPR-Cas12a systems are called AcrV proteins. Recent structural and biochemical studies have shown that AcrVA proteins inhibit Cas12a through highly different mechanisms. AcrVA1 induces cleavage of Cas12a-bound crRNA. AcrVA2 recognizes the nascent Cas12a polypeptide and promotes translation-dependent degradation of cas12a mRNA. AcrVA3 directly cleaves double-stranded DNA and indirectly reduces Cas12a activity. AcrVA4 allosterically blocks target DNA binding, whereas AcrVA5-AcrVA8 inhibit Cas12a by acetylating important lysine residues. These studies provide a structural basis for using AcrVA proteins as potential Cas12a off-switches. Importantly, AcrV proteins may reduce off-target effects by limiting the strength and duration of Cas12a activity after sufficient on-target editing has occurred. In this mini review, we summarize the structural mechanisms of AcrVA proteins and critically discuss the evidence and experimental requirements for their potential use in controlled Cas12a-based microbial engineering.

title: Molecular mechanisms of AcrVA-mediated Cas12a inhibition and their potential applications.

abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) therapeutics have rapidly emerged as a transformative approach for treating a range of health challenges. Accelerated by the success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccines during the COVID-19 pandemic, this platform holds promise beyond immunisation for the transient expression of therapeutic proteins in targeted tissues. Despite this promise, non-invasive delivery of mRNA-encoded cargo to the brain remains a challenge, as most peptide drugs do not pass the blood-brain barrier. Here, we present the development of an intranasal mRNA-LNP therapeutic that drives production of neurotrophic factors in the nasal epithelium and delivery of the encoded protein to the brain. As a proof of concept, we demonstrate that intranasal delivery of mRNA encoding the neurogenic factor BDNF (Brain Derived Neurotrophic Factor) enhances memory performance in both aged mice and a transgenic mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. This approach offers a promising platform for delivering therapeutic proteins to the brain and opens new avenues for treating age-related and neurodegenerative disorders.

title: Bdnf mRNA-LNP Drives Nasal Epithelial BDNF Production and Improves Cognition in Aged and Alzheimer's Disease Mouse Models.

abstract: The blood-brain barrier (BBB) and blood-brain tumor barrier (BBTB) severely limited drug delivery into the brain, while aberrant aerobic glycolysis in the tumor microenvironment caused excessive lactate accumulation and drove immunosuppression. These factors together constituted the core obstacles to glioblastoma (GBM) therapy. From the perspective of metabolism-immune crosstalk, we engineered a brain‑targeted nucleic acid nanosphere (TE@siP‑DNS/DOX) featuring high BBB/BBTB penetrability, which orchestrated a "triple‑linked" strategy integrating glycolysis blockade, immune microenvironment remodeling, and synergistic therapeutic potentiation. The nanosphere was constructed with a self‑assembled core of PKM2‑targeting siRNA and framework nucleic acids loaded with doxorubicin (DOX), shielded by a biomimetic shell of T7 peptide‑modified macrophage extracellular vesicles. Leveraging transcytosis and T7‑mediated active targeting, TE@siP‑DNS/DOX efficiently traversed the barriers and preferentially accumulated at tumor sites. DOX simultaneously provoked chemotherapy and immunogenic cell death, igniting robust CD8⁺ T cell‑mediated antitumor immunity, whereas siRNA‑mediated PKM2 silencing curtailed glycolysis, lessened lactate production, rewired metabolic circuitry, and forced macrophage polarization toward the M1 antitumor phenotype, thereby dismantling the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (iTME). Transcriptomic analysis further confirmed that metabolic and immune-related pathways were significantly enriched following TE@siP-DNS/DOX treatment, providing transcriptional evidence for its dual modulation of the metabolic-immune feedback loop. In vivo studies substantiated that TE@siP‑DNS/DOX markedly inhibited tumor growth and prolonged survival in orthotopic GBM-bearing mice. Collectively, this nanoplatform, through a synergistic feedback loop integrating metabolic regulation and immune activation, provides a good therapeutic strategy and research paradigm for enhanced glioma therapy. STATEMENT OF SIGNIFICANCE: Glioblastoma therapy is impeded by a multifaceted barrier system encompassing the blood-brain barrier, metabolic dysregulation, lactate accumulation, and immunosuppression. Here, we engineered a brain-targeted nucleic acid nanosphere that integrates glycolysis blockade, immune remodeling, and chemotherapeutic sensitization via a single platform. By combining PKM2 silencing with doxorubicin-loaded framework nucleic acids and T7-modified macrophage vesicles, the nanosphere achieves efficient barrier penetration, lactate reduction, M1 macrophage repolarization, and immunogenic cell death. This metabolism-immune feedback loop synergistically suppresses orthotopic tumors and extends survival. Our study provides a paradigm for treating brain tumors through concurrent metabolic reprogramming and antitumor immunity, offering a translatable strategy for overcoming therapy resistance in glioblastoma.

title: Macrophage Extracellular Vesicle-Camouflaged Framework Nucleic Acid Nanospheres Reprogram Lactate Metabolism-Immune Feedback Loops for Synergistic Chemoimmunotherapy of Glioblastoma.

abstract: Interface integration failure after implanting bone repair material is a core challenge in treating bone defects. This study aimed to investigate the molecular mechanism by which endothelial cell-derived small extracellular vesicles (EC-sEVs) deliver lncRNA DLX1 (lncDLX1) to regulate the osteogenic differentiation of BMSCs through both in vitro and in vivo experiments. The results showed that lncDLX1 expression was significantly downregulated in an inflammatory microenvironment and that overexpression of lncDLX1 promoted BMSC osteogenic differentiation while inhibiting inflammatory responses. Mechanistic studies revealed that lncDLX1 binds to RBMX, which then transcriptionally activates β-catenin expression and enhances its mRNA stability by binding to the CTNNB1 promoter region, thereby activating the Wnt/β-catenin pathway. Functional experiments confirmed that EC-sEVscould be effectively taken up by BMSCs and functionally deliver lncDLX1, and GW4869 treatment attenuated this regulatory effect, supporting the involvement of sEVs. In vivo experiments showed that hydroxyapatite materials loaded with lncDLX1-overexpressing BMSCs significantly promoted bone repair in a rat femoral defect model. In summary, this study reveals the central role of the EC-sEVs/lncDLX1/RBMX/Wnt/β-catenin signaling axis in bone repair, providing a new theoretical basis for the development of sEV-based lncRNA bone repair strategies.

abstract: This phase II trial evaluates tamoxifen, with or without omega-3 fatty acids, for reducing risk of breast cancer among postmenopausal and overweight or obese women who are at increased risk of developing breast cancer. Tamoxifen is a selective estrogen receptor modulator. It works by blocking the effects of the hormone estrogen in the breast. Tamoxifen is approved by the Food and Drug Administration for prevention of breast cancer in women at increased risk. Omega-3 fatty acids have been shown to decrease the amount of fats made in the liver. Omega-3 fatty acids may work to prevent cancer in overweight or obese individuals. Tamoxifen with or without omega-3 fatty acids may be effective at reducing risk of breast cancer among women who are postmenopausal, overweight or obese, and at increased risk.
description:
PRIMARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To investigate average change in serum adiponectin within the low dose tamoxifen (LDTAM) + high dose omega-3-acid ethyl esters (omega-3 fatty acids) arm.

II. To study the beneficial effects of addition of high dose omega-3 fatty acids to LDTAM by comparing the relative difference in change in serum adiponectin in overweight and obese high-risk postmenopausal women randomized to 6 months of LDTAM or LDTAM + high dose omega-3 fatty acids.

SECONDARY OBJECTIVES:

I. To determine effect of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on insulin resistance, insulin sensitivity, and insulin secretory function (homeostatic model assessment for insulin resistance \[HOMA-IR\], homeostatic model assessment of insulin sensitivity \[HOMA%S\] homeostatic model assessment of beta cell function, \[HOMA%B\]), respectively.

II. To determine effect of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acid on benign breast tissue estrogen response gene index (ERGI).

EXPLANATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Effect of change in red blood cell (RBC) omega-3:omega-6 fatty acid ratio on within arm change in blood adiponectin.

II. Effect of change in RBC omega-3:omega-6 fatty acid ratio on within arm change in tissue ERGI.

III. Effect of baseline bioavailable estradiol on within arm change in blood adiponectin.

IV. Effect of baseline and 6-month bioavailable estradiol on within arm change in tissue ERGI.

V. Effect of 6-month tamoxifen active metabolites (endoxifen and 4-hydroxy \[4OH\] tamoxifen) on change in ERGI.

VI. Effect of eicosapentaenoic acid/docosahexaenoic acid (EPA/DHA) dietary intake as measured by DHA Food Frequency Questionnaire on RBC omega 3:6 fatty acid ratio change.

EXPLORATORY OBJECTIVES:

I. Assess within arm effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on serum triglycerides.

II. Assess within arm effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on adiponectin:leptin ratio.

III. Assess within arm effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on anterior gradient protein 2 homolog (AGR2) messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA).

IV. Assess within effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on forkhead box A1 (FOXA1) protein (immunohistochemistry \[IHC\]).

V. Assess within arm effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on AGR2 protein (IHC).

VI. Assess effects of LDTAM +/- high dose omega-3 fatty acids on Ki-67 (IHC) in individuals with \> 500 cells in baseline ThinPrep and measurable baseline Ki-67.

OUTLINE: Participants are randomized to 1 of 2 groups.

GROUP 1: Participants receive tamoxifen by mouth (PO) once daily (QD) for 180 days in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Participants may continue to receive tamoxifen PO QD for up to 60 additional days in the case of scheduling delays. Participants also undergo mammography at screening and undergo random periareolar fine needle aspiration (RPFNA) and collection of blood samples at screening and on study.

GROUP 2: Participants receive tamoxifen PO QD and omega-3 fatty acids PO twice daily (BID) for 180 days in the absence of unacceptable toxicity. Participants may continue to receive tamoxifen PO QD and omega-3 fatty acids PO BID for up to 60 additional days in the case of scheduling delays. Participants also undergo mammography at screening and undergo RPFNA and collection of blood samples at screening and on study.

After completion of study intervention, participants are followed up at 21-35 days.

abstract: Phase 1/2, Open-label, Multi-center, First-in-human Study of the Safety, Tolerability, Pharmacokinetics, Pharmacodynamics and Anti-tumor Activity of STX-001 Delivered by Intratumoral Injection in Patients with Advanced Solid Tumors as a Monotherapy or in Combination with Pembrolizumab. The study now includes a monotherapy cohort targeting visceral lesions and a separate Phase 2 monotherapy cohort for advanced melanoma.
description:
This open-label, Phase 1/2, first-in-human (FIH), multiple ascending dose and dose expansion study involves STX-001 administration, alone or in combination with pembrolizumab, to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK), pharmacodynamics (PD), and preliminary antitumor activity in patients with advanced cancers.

Phase 1 consists of 4 planned dose escalation cohorts of STX-001 delivered as a monotherapy (Cohorts 1m), 4 planned dose escalation monotherapy cohorts of STX-001 delivered as a combination therapy with pembrolizumab treatment given concurrently (Cohorts 1c), and an additional monotherapy cohort targeting visceral lesions (Cohort 1vm) that will be evaluated at 30ug, 100ug and 300ug. New patients will be enrolled in each dose escalation cohort.

Phase 2 consists of dose expansion cohorts in patients with 2 defined cancer types: triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) and melanoma. There will also be a monotherapy cohort for advanced melanoma. Phase 2 will evaluate STX-001 in combination with pembrolizumab; the recommended Phase 2 dose (RP2D) will be selected based on analysis of the totality of data from Phase 1 safety, tolerability, PK, PD and preliminary efficacy data.

abstract:
Background:

X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (XSCID) is a rare inherited disorder that affects the immune system. It is caused by a change in the IL2RG gene. Researchers are investigating a new type of gene therapy for people with XSCID. This technique, called base-edited stem cell transplants, involves collecting a person s own stem cells, editing the genes to repair IL2RG gene, and returning the edited cells to the person.

Objective:

To test base-edited stem cell transplants in people with XSCID.

Eligibility:

People aged 3 years and older with XSCID.

Design:

Participants will be screened. They will have a physical exam. They may give blood, urine, and stool samples. They may have tests of their heart and lung function. They may have fluid and cells drawn from their bone marrow.

Participants will undergo apheresis. Blood will be taken from the body through a needle inserted into 1 arm. The blood will pass through a machine that separates out the stem cells. The remaining blood will be returned to the body through a different needle. The collected stem cells will undergo gene editing.

Participants will be admitted to the hospital before treatment. They will receive a central line: A flexible tube will be inserted into a large vein. This tube will be used to administer drugs and draw blood during their stay. Before receiving the gene edited cells, participants will receive a reduced dose of busulfan, a drug that makes room in the bone marrow for the treated cells. The busulfan dose may be further adjusted for participants with significant organ damage. Alemtuzumab (Campath) may also be given to some participants to address certain immune problems involving donor T cells from a previous transplant.

The base-edited stem cells will be infused through the central line. Participants will remain in the hospital for at least 3 weeks while they recover.

Follow-up visits will continue for 15 years.

description:
Study Description:

This is a phase 1/2, non-randomized study of a single infusion of autologous hematopoietic stem/progenitor cells base-edited to repair interleukin 2 receptor gamma (IL2RG) mutations (BE-HSPC IL2RG) in 18 participants with X-linked severe combined immunodeficiency (X-SCID).

Primary Objective:

Evaluate the safety of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG in participants with X-SCID.

Secondary Objectives:

Evaluate efficacy of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG in participants with X-SCID.

Exploratory Objectives:

1. Evaluate off-target (OT) editing activity.
2. Compare outcomes of immune reconstitution with lentivector (LV) gene therapy.

Primary Endpoint:

Safety of treatment with BE-HSPC IL2RG, by quantifying frequency and severity of adverse events (AEs) related to study agent from infusion to 12 months after infusion.

Secondary Endpoints (24 months post-study agent infusion):

1. Percentage of participants with \>=5% mutation-repaired myeloid cells.
2. Editing efficiency in peripheral blood cells (such as T, B, and natural killer \[NK\] cells).
3. Immune reconstitution:

   1. T, B, and NK cell number improvement from baseline.
   2. Emergence of naive T cells and CD31+ recent thymic emigrants.
   3. B-cell function: immunoglobulin (Ig) production.
   4. Specific responses to vaccines.
4. Clinical efficacy: improvement from baseline problems such as recurrent infection, chronic norovirus, protein-losing enteropathy, gastrointestinal complaints, growth failure, malnutrition, or immune dysregulation.
5. Frequency and severity of all study agent-related AEs and serious adverse events (SAEs) from time of study product infusion.

Exploratory Endpoints:

1. Evaluate for frequency of off-targets (OTs) by high-throughput sequencing (HTS) of the target mutation at 2 years post-infusion.
2. Compare rates of immune reconstitution with LV-X-SCID gene therapy.

abstract: ATR 1072 is an investigational medicine being studied in adults with PRKAG2 Syndrome. This study will evaluate the safety of ATR 1072 and how the body processes the drug. Researchers will also assess how ATR 1072 affects PRKAG2 activity and measures of heart disease.
description: ATR 1072 is an antibody-oligonucleotide conjugate (AOC) designed to reduce expression of PRKAG2 through targeted delivery of siRNA to cardiac tissue. This first-in-human, Phase 1/2, open-label, multicenter study will evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and exploratory efficacy of multiple doses of ATR 1072 in adults with PRKAG2 Syndrome. The study consists of a multiple ascending dose portion (Part A) followed by a dose-expansion cohort at the dose selected in (Part A). After completion of a 48-week treatment period, participants in Parts A and B enter a 42-week extension period followed by a post-treatment follow-up of up to 18 weeks. Approximately 37 participants will be enrolled globally.

abstract:
The Investigators have demonstrated in preclinical studies that RNA liposomes activate APCs, induce antigen-specific T cell immunity, and can supplant DCs in a cell therapy model for HGG and have shown feasibility and activity of this approach in preclinical models and in canine patients with a spontaneous malignant glioma. In one arm of this study, we will investigate the safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccines in pediatric patients with recurrent pHGG.

The investigators have also shown that intravenous administration of tumor mRNA loaded lipid particles (LPs) localizes primarily to lung, transfect antigen presenting cells (APCs) and lead to an activated T cell response for induction of anti-tumor immunity. In contrast to other formulations, RNA-LPs recruit multiple arms of the immune system (i.e. innate/adaptive), and remodel the systemic/intratumoral immune milieu, which remain potent barriers for vaccine, cellular, and checkpoint inhibiting immunotherapies. After only a single RNA-LP vaccine, the bulk of systemic and intratumoral dendritic cells (DCs) in mice display an activated phenotype; these activated DCs (harvested from tumors) expand antigen specific T cell immunity. In immunologically resistant pulmonary osteosacroma murine tumor models (i.e. K7M2), RNA-LPs induce robust anti-tumor efficacy in settings where immune checkpoint inhibitors (i.e. anti-PD-L1 therapy) do not confer therapeutic benefit. The investigators have already demonstrated safety of RNA-LPs in acute/chronic murine toxicity studies, and in client-owned canine trial.

In this study, we will investigate the manufacturing feasibility, safety and immunologic activity of RNA-LP vaccine in patients with recurrent pulmonary or unresectable osteosarcoma and recurrent pHGG.

abstract: This study aims to examine the long-term effect of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS), a non-invasive brain stimulation technique, on chronic headaches following mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI). rTMS has been shown to be effective in reducing chronic headaches without side effects commonly seen in medications, such as sleepiness and addiction. This study uses rTMS to manage chronic headaches to improve post-concussion symptoms and reduce the economic burden due to delayed recovery. This project aims to better identify biomarkers for diagnosis and prognosis and maximize recovery from mTBI.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized by cognitive decline, oxidative stress, and neuronal loss. Current pharmacological treatments provide only partial symptomatic relief. This study investigated the neuroprotective effects of the petroleum ether fraction of Teucrium polium (T. polium), administered in both free and lipid nanoparticle formulations (T. polium-LNP), in a rat model of AD-like pathology induced by intracerebroventricular streptozotocin (ICV-STZ).
METHODS: Adult male Wistar rats were divided into five groups: Control, ICV-STZ, ICV-STZ + Memantine, ICV-STZ + T. polium, and ICV-STZ + T. polium-LNP. Cognitive function was assessed using the Morris water maze (MWM) and novel object recognition (NOR) tests. Serum oxidative stress markers-including malondialdehyde (MDA), total antioxidant capacity (TAC), and superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity-were measured. Hippocampal CA1 histopathology and hippocampal mRNA expression of Bax, Bcl-2, and p53 were also evaluated.
RESULTS: The ICV-STZ-induced AD-like model was associated with memory impairment, increased serum MDA levels, reduced TAC levels and SOD activity, and hippocampal CA1 neuronal damage, accompanied by increased Bax and p53 expression and decreased Bcl-2 expression. Treatment with T. polium and T. polium-LNP improved cognitive performance, particularly spatial memory in the MWM, and attenuated several pathological changes. Both treatments reduced serum MDA levels and decreased CA1 neuronal degeneration.
CONCLUSION: In this experimental AD-like rat model, both formulations of T. polium were associated with improvements in cognitive performance, serum oxidative status markers, and hippocampal tissue changes. Although T. polium-LNP showed numerically greater effects on several outcomes, direct comparisons between the free T. polium extract and T. polium-LNP were statistically significant only for CA1 neuronal damage. Further mechanistic and long-term studies are needed to clarify the potential relevance of these findings to AD-related neuroprotection.

abstract: Background: Glioblastoma (GBM) is highly refractory to standard therapies, including anti-angiogenic agents such as bevacizumab. While bevacizumab prunes tumor vasculature, it exacerbates intratumoral hypoxia, which drives a metabolically resilient phenotype that limits survival benefits. This study aimed to identify the metabolic dependencies underlying GBM adaptation to hypoxia and to evaluate whether targeting these dependencies could enhance the antitumor efficacy of bevacizumab. Methods: We analyzed the spatial distribution of key metabolites in GBM patients and orthotopic xenograft mouse models using magnetic resonance spectroscopy and chemical shift imaging. A dual-vector hypoxia fate-mapping system paired with an in vivo genome-wide clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats (CRISPR)-CRISPR-associated protein 9 (Cas9) knockout screen was employed to identify metabolic vulnerabilities within the hypoxic niche. Metabolic flux was analyzed utilizing 13C5-labeled glutamine tracers. The molecular mechanisms governing solute carrier family 38 member 2 (SLC38A2) regulation were investigated using chromatin immunoprecipitation, cycloheximide chase assays, liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, and co-immunoprecipitation. The efficacy of targeting SLC38A2 was evaluated through structure-based virtual screening and in vivo orthotopic xenograft models treated concurrently with zonisamide and bevacizumab. Results: Imaging and tissue metabolite analyses revealed a spatial metabolic mismatch in the hypoxic tumor core, characterized by lactate accumulation alongside glutamine depletion. In vivo CRISPR-Cas9 screening identified SLC38A2 as an essential metabolic dependency for GBM cell survival under hypoxic stress. Under hypoxic conditions, hypoxia-inducible factor 1 alpha (HIF-1α) promoted SLC38A2 transcription, while elevated lactate stabilized the SLC38A2 protein through alanyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (AARS1)-mediated lactylation at Lys472. These changes were accompanied by increased glutamine uptake and glutathione biosynthesis, reduced reactive oxygen species levels, and decreased mitochondrial-fission-mediated apoptosis. Pharmacological screening identified the US Food and Drug Administration-approved, brain-penetrant anticonvulsant zonisamide as an inhibitor of SLC38A2. In orthotopic GBM xenograft models, combined treatment with zonisamide and bevacizumab markedly suppressed tumor growth compared with bevacizumab alone. Conclusions: This study defines a spatially organized lactate-glutamine metabolic axis essential for hypoxic adaptation in GBM. The dual transcriptional and posttranslational up-regulation of SLC38A2 represents a critical survival mechanism. This axis can be pharmacologically dismantled by zonisamide, offering a clinically actionable combinational strategy to overcome anti-angiogenic therapy resistance.

abstract: Amyloidosis comprises a group of systemic disorders caused by extracellular deposition of misfolded precursor proteins, leading to progressive organ dysfunction. Cardiac amyloidosis, particularly transthyretin-related amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) has transitioned from a rare and underdiagnosed condition to a treatable disease, driven by major advances in diagnostic imaging, increased disease awareness, and the approval of disease-modifying therapies. These therapies target transthyretin (TTR) stabilization and amyloid production or deposition and have led to an evolving therapeutic landscape. As therapeutic efficacy is greatest in earlier disease stages, timely recognition is crucial. Effective management of ATTR-CM requires structured screening of high-risk populations, multidisciplinary collaboration, and longitudinal follow-up. This review provides a practical, clinician-focused framework that addresses clinical presentation and "red flags" to facilitate early detection. It offers a comprehensive overview of the diagnostic pathway, including (AI-enabled) electrocardiography analysis, (non-)invasive imaging modalities, biomarkers, and genetic testing. Additionally, emerging therapeutic strategies are discussed, encompassing supportive heart failure management, amyloid-specific treatments such as TTR stabilizers and gene silencers, and novel approaches including fibril depletion and gene-editing therapies. As the therapeutic paradigm shifts from disease stabilization toward potential reversal, early diagnosis and personalized treatment strategies are essential to improve prognosis and quality of life in patients with cardiac amyloidosis.

title: Transforming cardiac amyloidosis care: navigating the evolving diagnostic and therapeutic landscape.

abstract: Metabolic disorders are increasingly associated with intestinal dysfunction and colorectal diseases, yet the pathological characteristics and underlying mechanisms of intestinal injury under metabolic stress remain poorly understood. Here, we established a transgenic (TG) Bama pig model by CRISPR/Cas9-mediated knock-in of three humanized susceptibility genes and subjected the pigs to a high-fat, high-sugar diet (HFHSD) for 4, 8, or 12 months to investigate metabolic disorder-associated colonic dysfunction. HFHSD intervention induced marked alterations in serum biochemical parameters and disrupted colonic mucosal architecture, characterized by glandular disorganization and crypt distortion. Colonic tissues from TG pigs exhibited reduced populations of goblet cells, CD8⁺ T cells, and CD79A⁺ B cells, accompanied by pronounced activation of mitophagy, indicating impaired epithelial barrier integrity and mucosal immune homeostasis. In parallel, microbial diversity and IgA levels were reduced in the colonic contents of TG pigs, accompanied by an increased abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria, particularly Escherichia-Shigella. Metabolomic profiling of colonic contents further revealed significant alterations in the intestinal metabolic landscape, including decreased levels of isobutyric acid and isovaleric acid and an increased level of myristic acid, a metabolite associated with autophagy-related processes. Collectively, these findings demonstrate that metabolic disorders are associated with coordinated alterations in colonic mucosal integrity, mucosal immunity, mitochondrial quality control, gut microbiota, and intestinal metabolism. The humanized TG Bama pig model provides a clinically relevant large-animal platform for investigating the pathophysiology of metabolic disorder-associated colonic diseases and may facilitate the development and preclinical evaluation of therapeutic strategies targeting intestinal dysfunction.

title: A Transgenic Pig Model for human Metabolic Disorders Defines the relationship between the colon pathological phenotype of metabolic disease, the microbiota and the intestinal barrier.

abstract: C-to-G base editors (CGBEs) offer the potential to correct 11% of pathogenic single-nucleotide variants. While APOBEC-based CGBEs are highly efficient, they are limited by high indel rates and off-target activity. In contrast, TadA-based CGBEs offer greater precision but currently suffer from suboptimal editing efficiency. In this study, we first developed zCGBE, a TadA-based variant that achieves editing efficiency comparable to APOBEC-based editors while maintaining low Cas-independent off-target activity. To further reduce residual on-target indels, we engineered mi-zCGBE by fusing Brex27, a 36-amino-acid-long RAD51-recruiting peptide, to zCGBE. Mi-zCGBE preserves high C-to-G editing capacity and low Cas9-independent off-target activity while significantly reducing both on-target indels and guide-RNA-dependent off-target effects. We demonstrated the potential utility of mi-zCGBE by correcting the CFTR-N1303K mutation in Cystic Fibrosis patient-derived bronchial epithelial cells, achieving high rates of base correction and minimal indels or off-target edits, leading to restored CFTR protein expression and functional chloride channel activity. These results establish mi-zCGBE as an efficient and precise tool for gene editing research and future therapeutic applications.

abstract: Like many other immune cell types, natural killer (NK) cells exhibit impaired functionality in people with HIV (PWH), limiting their ability to efficiently target and eliminate HIV-infected cells and contributing to the persistence of the HIV reservoir. Recently, adoptive NK cell therapy using activated or engineered NK cells has emerged as a promising immunotherapeutic strategy for cancer; however, its application to HIV remains in the early stages of development. NK cells primarily rely on interleukin-15 (IL-15) signaling for their development, survival, and maintenance, and dysregulated IL-15 signaling has been reported in PWH. We hypothesized that simultaneous enhancement of IL-15 and IL-15 receptor alpha (IL-15Rα) expression would improve NK cell effector function and promote clearance of HIV reservoir. Utilizing dCas9-VPR-mediated multiplex CRISPR activation (CRISPRa), we successfully upregulated both IL-15 and IL-15Rα expression in the same primary NK cells without altering the genomic sequence. CRISPRa-treated NK cells displayed increased IL-15 and IL-15Rα transcript levels, as measured by RT-qPCR and significantly elevated surface expression of IL-15Rα, as determined by flow cytometry. Enhanced IL-15/IL-15Rα expression increased NK cell metabolic activity and cytotoxicity against target K562 cells, a chronic myelogenous leukemia cell line, indicating improved effector function. Furthermore, in co-culture experiments using an HIV-positive T-cell line, IL-15/IL-15Rα-CRISPRa-treated NK cells demonstrated enhanced target cell elimination and increased secretion of IFN-γ. Together, these findings provide a proof of concept that multiplex CRISPRa can be used to enhance NK cell function, representing a novel strategy to improve persistence and therapeutic efficacy in HIV and other disease settings.

abstract: Small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) often exhibit a neuroendocrine lineage identity marked by high expression of Delta-like ligand 3 (DLL3). Because DLL3 shows minimal expression in normal adult tissues, it serves as an SCLC-selective tumor antigen and is the basis for clinically efficacious targeted therapies. Understanding the mechanisms that regulate DLL3 expression is therefore critical for advancing therapeutic strategies in this disease. Here, we performed transcription factor-focused and genome-wide CRISPR screens to identify regulators of DLL3 expression in SCLC. Both approaches converged on POU2F1 as a top activator of DLL3 in this tumor context. Despite its ubiquitous expression, we identify an SCLC-specific role for POU2F1 in activating DLL3 and a broader set of neuroendocrine lineage genes. Epigenomic analyses reveal tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 motifs within the DLL3 promoter that underlie the functional cooperativity between POU2F1 and the neuroendocrine master regulator ASCL1 for high-level DLL3 expression in SCLC. We provide evidence that tandem POU2F1-ASCL1 elements are part of a cis-regulatory code for the lung neuroendocrine cell fate. Together, these findings define a previously unrecognized transcriptional logic controlling DLL3 expression and establish POU2F1 as a context-specific regulator of neuroendocrine lineage in SCLC.

abstract: Through a genome-wide forward CRISPR/Cas9 screen in interleukin-3 (IL3)-dependent Ba/F3 cells, we identified osteoclastogenesis-associated transmembrane protein 1 (OSTM1) as a previously unrecognized tumor suppressor. Analysis of patient datasets revealed that OSTM1 is frequently deleted or downregulated in human B-cell malignancies (BCM). In mice, Cd19-Cre-driven B cell-specific monoallelic or biallelic deletion of Ostm1 cooperated with Cdkn2a loss to drive lymphomagenesis with near-complete penetrance. Mechanistically, OSTM1 directly interacts with phosphodiesterase 3B (PDE3B) and promotes its proteasomal degradation. Because PDE3B hydrolyzes cyclic AMP (cAMP), loss of OSTM1 stabilizes PDE3B, leading to suppression of tumor-suppressive cAMP-dependent PKA/CREB signaling and promotion of oncogenic transformation. Consistent with this mechanism, PDE3B is frequently amplified or upregulated in BCM, and expression of CREB/CREBBP transcriptional targets correlates positively with OSTM1 expression but inversely with PDE3B across BCM cohorts. Importantly, silencing Pde3b reverses oncogenic transformation driven by Ostm1 loss. Together, these findings establish OSTM1 as a tumor suppressor and uncover an OSTM1/PDE3B/cAMP signaling axis that restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis and may represent a therapeutically actionable vulnerability.
