title: OSTM1 restrains B-cell lymphomagenesis by promoting PDE3B degradation and activating cAMP/PKA/CREB signaling.

abstract:
This study evaluates whether a 12-month supervised progressive resistance training program improves lean body mass and metabolic health in obese North Indian adults aged 35-60 years. Asian Indians are uniquely predisposed to sarcopenic obesity-the coexistence of excess body fat and reduced muscle mass-which significantly increases the risk of type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

Participants will be stratified into High-Ratio and Low-Ratio groups based on their baseline Myostatin/Follistatin (MSTN/FST) ratio, an biological index of muscle catabolism versus growth. Half of the participants in each stratum will undergo a 12-month supervised resistance training program, while the other half will receive standard lifestyle advice. The primary goal is to determine whether baseline MSTN/FST ratio predicts the extent of muscle mass gain and whether reducing this ratio mediates improvements in insulin resistance and systemic inflammation.

institutions.label: Indian Council of Medical Research

description:
Background \& Scientific Rationale: Sarcopenic obesity is a major driver of cardiometabolic risk in Asian Indians due to low baseline lean mass combined with high visceral adiposity. Myostatin (MSTN) acts as a primary negative regulator of muscle growth, whereas follistatin (FST) acts as its circulating antagonist. Previous genetic research demonstrates that gain-of-function Myostatin gene variants are strongly associated with lower lean body mass and increased adiposity in North Indians. This trial prospectively tests whether the serum MSTN/FST ratio functions as a precision biomarker to stratify exercise response and guide targeted exercise interventions.

Study Objectives:

Determine the efficacy of a 12-month supervised resistance training program on total lean body mass (LBM) and physical performance compared to lifestyle control, testing for treatment interaction across baseline MSTN/FST strata.

Characterize the molecular adaptations of the myostatin axis by measuring serum myostatin, follistatin, MSTN/FST ratio, and peripheral blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) MSTN mRNA expression at baseline and 12 months.

Assess whether reductions in the MSTN/FST ratio mediate improvements in insulin resistance (HOMA-IR), systemic inflammatory markers (IL-6, TNF-α, hsCRP), and muscle quality.

Trial Design \& Interventions: A single-center, ratio-stratified, 1:1 parallel-group randomized controlled superiority trial of 200 obese North Indian adults.

Resistance Training Arm (n=100): 3 supervised sessions per week (60 minutes per session) at 70-80% 1-repetition maximum (1RM) using progressive resistance overload reassessed every 8 weeks.

Control Arm (n=100): Standard individualized dietary and physical activity advice per national guidelines without supervised exercise sessions.

Outcome Assessments: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) for total LBM, appendicular lean mass, and body fat percentage; handgrip dynamometry and 1RM testing for strength; quantitative ELISA for serum biomarkers; real-time qRT-PCR (2-ΔΔCt method) for PBMC MSTN mRNA expression; and standardized biochemical panels for glycemic and inflammatory profiles.

abstract: The growing recognition of base editing as a precise genome-engineering strategy for single‑nucleotide conversions without double‑strand breaks has increased interest in its application to animal agriculture, where many economically important traits are influenced by single nucleotide variants. Although recent engineering efforts have broadened the targeting scope, improved editing precision, and reduced off‑target activity, major challenges remain in translating these tools to livestock and aquaculture species, particularly with respect to delivery, mosaicism, germline transmission, and breeding-scale deployment. In this review, we outline the development of cytosine, adenine, dual, and mitochondrial base editors, and discuss their advances in livestock and fish, including trait-oriented editing in pigs and cattle, rapid functional validation in model fish, and early proof-of-concept studies in aquaculture species. We further discuss the emerging potential of mitochondrial DNA base editing for animal breeding and evaluate the extent to which current advances support the broader goal of precision breeding and sustainable animal production.

abstract:
INTRODUCTION: Mitophagy, the selective clearance of defective mitochondria via the autophagy-lysosome pathway, is essential for maintaining mitochondrial health and cellular homeostasis. Dysregulation of mitophagy is strongly implicated in aging-related pathologies, including neurodegenerative diseases (Alzheimer's, Parkinson's), cancer, and metabolic disorders, highlighting the significance of elucidating its regulatory mechanisms. While existing methods using exogenous reporters enable genome-wide and high-throughput screening for mitophagy regulators, they constrain discoveries to specific pathways and introduce artifacts through ectopic expression.
OBJECTIVES: To overcome these limitations, we developed an effective and rapid platform for identifying mitophagy modulators by targeting endogenous proteins.
METHODS: Using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, we engineered HeLa cells expressing small molecular tags (GFP or NanoLuc) fused to the C-terminal of ATP5B, a mitochondrial inner membrane protein. Genome-wide screening for mitophagy regulatory genes were performed using a genome-wide CRISPR library coupled with flow cytometry. Additionally, an FDA-approved kinase inhibitor library was used to screen for mitophagy inducers. To evaluate the efficacy of a screened drug in Alzheimer's disease, cognitive behavior, pathological features and mitophagy events in 3 × Tg-AD mice with or without treatment were examined using the Morris water maze assay, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM).
RESULTS: These ATP5B-tagging cells provided a robust readout of mitophagy and enabled high-throughput genetic or pharmacological screening. With this platform, we identified several promising genes that regulate mitophagy and are significantly associated with Alzheimer's disease. Moreover, the FDA-approved drug Flupentixol emerged as a novel mitophagy inducer that acts by promoting adenosine monophosphate-activated protein kinase (AMPK) localization to mitochondria and exhibited strong therapeutic potential in a model of Alzheimer's disease.
CONCLUSION: This study establishes a novel system for identifying mitophagy modulators, with the potential to accelerate the discovery of therapeutic strategies for Alzheimer's disease.

title: Identification of mitophagy inducers for Alzheimer's disease via high-throughput endogenous ATP5B tagging system.

abstract: The rising global burden of depression necessitates novel mechanistic insights and therapeutic targets. Voltage-gated sodium channel β2-subunit (Navβ2, coded by SCN2B) has been implicated in neuropsychiatric disorders, yet its role in depression remains unexplored. Here, we identify SCN2B as a previously unrecognized driver of depression-like pathophysiology. Using SCN2B-overexpressing (SCN2B-OV) mice across different ages (1, 12, and 20 months) and CRISPR- engineered Navβ2V173A,V175K mice with selective reduction of the Navβ2 intracellular domain (NICD), we combined behavioral phenotyping, electrophysiology, neurotransmitter profiling, and molecular analyses, with chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS) as an environmental challenge. SCN2B-OV mice exhibited accelerated depression-like phenotypes, including anhedonia (sucrose preference 52.42% reduction, P<0.05), behavioral despair (forced swim test immobility 67.42% increase, P<0.05), and cognitive deficits (Y-maze alternation 50.90% reduction, P<0.05), independent of natural aging. Electrophysiologically, SCN2B overexpression induced a striking prefrontal-hippocampal imbalance: prefrontal cortex (PFC) became hyperexcitable (glutamate release increased by 64.7%; sEPSC amplitude increased 2.05-fold, P<0.05), whereas the hippocampus showed synaptic suppression (GABA release reduced by 32.65%; sIPSC frequency reduced by 66.67%, P<0.05). Mechanistically, SCN2B overexpression suppressed BDNF/TrkB/PI3K/AKT signaling axis (BDNF reduced by 53.17%; p-TrkB reduced by 63.62%, P<0.05), accompanied by decreased synaptic proteins (PSD95 43.45%, synapsin I 40.31%, P<0.05). Remarkably, NICD-reduced Navβ2V173A,V175K mice were fully resistant to CUMS-induced behavioral and neurotransmitter deficits, establishing NICD as a critical mediator of stress vulnerability. Collectively, these findings unravel a causal pathway in which SCN2B overexpression drives NICD-dependent suppression of BDNF signaling, leading to region-specific excitatory/inhibitory imbalance, synaptic disintegration, and depression-like phenotypes. Targeting Navβ2 proteolysis to block NICD generation may thus represent a novel therapeutic strategy for mood disorders.

title: SCN2B Drives Depression-like Phenotypes in Mice by Suppressing BDNF Signaling via Its Intracellular Domain NICD.

abstract: Circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) has emerged as an important biomarker for early cancer diagnosis and therapeutic monitoring; however, the ultrasensitive detection of low-abundance single-nucleotide variations (SNVs) remains highly challenging. Herein, we developed an autocatalytic split-crRNA Cas12a fluorescence platform, termed AutoSCas, for highly sensitive detection of EGFR L858R mutant ctDNA. Upon recognition of trace EGFR L858R ctDNA, activated split-crRNA Cas12a (SCas12a) cleaved the loop region of a cascade hairpin probe, resulting in the release of functional spacer RNA (sRNA) molecules. The liberated sRNA further activated additional SCas12a complexes in the presence of assistant DNA, thereby establishing a positive-feedback autocatalytic nucleic acid circuit for exponential-like signal amplification. Simultaneously, a phosphorothioate-modified G-quadruplex hairpin probe was introduced as a low-background "signal-on" fluorescence reporter. Activated SCas12a continuously cleaved the loop region of the probe, releasing phosphorothioate-modified G-quadruplex that subsequently bound Thioflavin T to generate strong fluorescence signals. Benefiting from the synergistic integration of autocatalytic amplification and low-background signals, AutoSCas achieved ultrasensitive and highly specific ctDNA detection with a detection limit as low as 2 aM. Therefore, AutoSCas platform provides a pre-amplification-free strategy for highly sensitive SNV analysis and expands the design of split-crRNA-based CRISPR sensing systems.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Hypertension remains a leading cause of global morbidity and mortality, yet current therapeutic strategies lack sustained efficacy and long-term stability. Our study aimed to construct a humanized rodent model for drugs development especially currently prevalent small interfering RNA medication.
METHODS: A humanized hypertensive mouse model was generated by subcutaneous injection of neonatal mice with adeno-associated viruses encoding hAGT (human angiotensinogen) and hRENIN (human renin). Blood pressure was monitored weekly via tail-cuff plethysmography. Expression of hAGT and hRENIN was assessed by ELISA, Western blot, and reverse transcription quantitative polymerase chain reaction. Cardiac function was evaluated by echocardiography at 4 and 6 months postinjection. Hypertension-associated comorbidities were examined through histological analysis and ELISA. A modified N-acetylgalactosamine-conjugated small interfering RNA targeting human hepatic AGT (GalNAc-siAGT) was screened and subcutaneously administered to humanized hypertensive mice, either alone or in combination with valsartan, to evaluate therapeutic efficacy.
RESULTS: The dual adeno-associated virus-induced humanized hypertensive model exhibited a sustained hypertension for 6 months and manifested prevalent comorbidities, including heart failure and kidney disease. This modified GalNAc-siAGT demonstrated significant activity in knocking down hAGT both in vitro and in vivo. Only a single subcutaneous injection of GalNAc-siAGT in humanized hypertensive mice led to a sustained reduction in blood pressure lasting for 2 months, accompanied by cardio- and renoprotective effects. Moreover, combining GalNAc-siAGT with the renin-angiotensin system blocker, valsartan, significantly enhanced therapeutic efficacy.
CONCLUSIONS: Our study validated the antihypertensive therapeutic effect of GalNAc-siAGT in a humanized hypertensive murine model while highlighting the translational potential of this model for clinical drug development.

abstract:
The purpose of this study is to assess the safety profile of intramuscular injections of the Acne mRNA vaccine at 3 dose levels compared with placebo in 12 to 17 years old participants with moderate to severe acne.

An early safety data review (ESDR) will be conducted after each subcohort has completed an injection round; enrollment of the next higher dose level subcohort or progression of a subcohort to the subsequent injection round will only proceed if no safety concerns are identified. This sequential process will allow a cautious approach to vaccine injection in the adolescent population.

Study details are as follows:

* Before being enrolled in the study, participants complete a 4-week (ie, 1-month) screening period during which they will be called over the telephone approximately in the middle of the screening period to check they are not using prohibited medications and to remind them about the facial hygiene requirements.
* Once the screening period has been completed, the study duration will be up to 13 months for each participant
* Participants will be invited to a long-term extension study through a separate protocol.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: The success of mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) platforms has prompted significant interest in their application against bacterial pathogens. However, adapting these platforms requires optimising host-expressed antigen structure to ensure robust immunogenicity. While membrane anchoring enhances the efficacy of viral mRNA vaccines, its application in bacterial mRNA platforms remains largely unexplored. Plague, caused by the Gram-negative bacterium Yersinia pestis, has been one of the most devastating diseases throughout human history. Despite extensive studies, there are no licenced vaccines available.
METHODS: We developed a bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccine against Y. pestis, utilising the major antigens F1 and LcrV (5 μg of each mRNA). We evaluated glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI)-anchored and transmembrane (TM) variants alongside secreted native and hFc-conjugated formats to assess immunological profiles and determine protective efficacy in a murine model of pneumonic plague.
FINDINGS: Membrane-tethering of F1 and LcrV antigens improved overall immunogenicity. Whereas secreted native and hFc-conjugated variants elicited predominantly cell-mediated and serological immune responses, respectively, the membrane-anchored bivalent mRNA vaccine generated a robust, protective immune response. This dual humoural and cellular immunity facilitated robust (87.5%, 7/8 mice) protection following a single-dose vaccination.
INTERPRETATION: By progressing towards the single-dose biodefense benchmark prioritised by the World Health Organisation Target Product Profile, this membrane-anchored construct emerges as a promising translational candidate for a rapid-response plague vaccine. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that extending established antigen-tethering strategies to bacterial targets may be a highly effective approach for generating the potent immunity required to overcome complex bacterial infections.
FUNDING: This research was supported by the Israeli Science Foundation (grants 2012/20, 842/25), the Lewis Trust and the Shmunis Family Trust.

title: A single-dose membrane-anchored F1/LcrV mRNA vaccine confers protection against pneumonic plague: a preclinical study.

abstract: Glutaric aciduria type I (GA-1) is a severe metabolic disorder caused by a deficiency of glutaryl-CoA dehydrogenase (GCDH), leading to accumulation of organic acids in the brain and resulting in striatal injury and progressive movement disorders. Although early diagnosis and dietary management reduce risk, one-third of patients still develop debilitating neurological complications. We previously demonstrated that liver-specific deletion of aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase (AASS), an upstream enzyme in lysine degradation, is a promising therapeutic strategy. Here, we tested an N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc)-conjugated siRNA against Aass. Treatment of neonatal Gcdh-/- mice rescued lethality and improved the brain pathology while reducing toxic metabolites in the brain and other organs. Serum biomarkers, including glutaric acid, 3-hydroxyglutaric acid, and glutarylcarnitine, predicted neurological outcomes, supporting their use for therapeutic monitoring. Although systemic metabolite concentrations declined, their urinary excretion remained elevated, consistent with a renal washout phenomenon and preserved excretory capacity. These findings demonstrate the potential of liver-targeted small interfering RNA (siRNA) therapy as a treatment for GA-1.

title: Rescue of glutaric aciduria type I by GalNAc-conjugated siRNA against aminoadipate semialdehyde synthase.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cryptosporidiosis is a major enteric disease affecting humans and animals worldwide, with severe consequences in young children and neonatal livestock, yet treatment options remain extremely limited. Benzoxaboroles have emerged as promising broad-spectrum antiparasitic compounds, but their mechanisms of action, molecular targets, and resistance pathways in Cryptosporidium spp. remain incompletely understood, limiting their optimal therapeutic deployment. We previously showed that the benzoxaborole AN3661 inhibits the endonuclease Cleavage and Polyadenylation Specificity Factor 3 (CPSF3) in Cryptosporidium hominis, likely by disrupting pre-mRNA processing and restricting parasite growth. Here, we further investigated the mode of action of AN3661 and compared it with two additional benzoxaboroles, AN13762 and AN7973.
METHODOLOGY: Cell culture assays combined with imaging-based quantification were used to assess drug activity and determine the impact of treatment on parasite growth and development. CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing was used to introduce a point mutation into Cryptosporidium parvum CPSF3 and evaluate resistance to benzoxaboroles in vitro and in vivo. Nanopore sequencing was performed to examine the effects of drug exposure on parasite mRNA processing.
PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We identified a single mutation in C. parvum CPSF3 (Y385N) that conferred strong resistance to AN3661. In contrast, this mutation did not reduce sensitivity to AN13762 or AN7973, which are also suspected to target CPSF3. All three benzoxaboroles impaired mRNA processing, a process mediated by the CPSF machinery, and exhibited parasiticidal activity, with pronounced effects during late-stage maturation of first-generation meronts, including inhibition of parasite egress; two compounds also affected gametogenesis. Notably, AN7973 controlled severe infection in susceptible mice challenged with the AN3661-resistant C. parvum CPSF3 Y385N mutant. In Toxoplasma gondii, AN7973 remained active against strains resistant to AN3661 and AN13762, supporting a distinct mechanism of action. Finally, AN3661 and AN7973 were active against Eimeria tenella, and AN3661 against Giardia duodenalis.
CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Together, these results identify a resistance mechanism affecting AN3661 in Cryptosporidium, and highlight AN7973 as a promising alternative compound with broad antiparasitic activity and efficacy against AN3661-resistant parasites.

title: Mechanistic insights into benzoxaborole activity against Cryptosporidium parvum: CPSF3 targeting genetically validated for AN3661, with implications for resistance.

abstract: The therapeutic potential of CRISPR/Cas genome editing has advanced the development of precision medicine; however, its clinical translation for many in vivo applications remains limited by challenges in achieving safe, efficient, and targeted delivery. Conventional viral vectors and synthetic nanocarriers are associated with challenges including immunogenicity, limited cargo capacity, prolonged nuclease expression, off-target effects, and manufacturing complexities. Engineered extracellular vesicles (EVs) are being investigated as alternative delivery carriers due to their biological origin, capacity for cargo encapsulation, and opportunities for surface functionalization. However, their biocompatibility, immunogenicity, and ability to cross biological barriers depend on vesicle source, formulation, and experimental conditions. This review provides a comprehensive overview of recent advances in the design of engineered EVs for CRISPR/Cas delivery, with a particular focus on strategies to improve cargo loading, targeting specificity, and therapeutic efficacy. We discuss the advantages and limitations of different CRISPR cargo formats, including plasmid DNA, mRNA, and ribonucleoprotein complexes, together with endogenous and exogenous loading approaches, hybrid EV platforms, and methods for enhancing intracellular delivery. Advances in EV surface engineering through genetic, chemical, physical, and biomimetic modifications are highlighted as strategies being investigated to improve tissue-specific delivery and functional cargo transport. The review also highlights emerging research directions, including CRISPR-EV theranostic platforms and the application of artificial intelligence to enhance CRISPR-EV therapeutic systems. Finally, key translational challenges, including scalable production, EV heterogeneity, cargo-loading efficiency, biodistribution, regulatory standardization, and quality control, are critically discussed. EV-mediated CRISPR delivery remains at an early preclinical stage, with clinical safety and therapeutic efficacy yet to be established. Further advances in EV engineering, cargo-loading strategies, and manufacturing standardization are needed to support its potential clinical translation.

title: Engineered Extracellular Vesicles (EVs) as Carriers for CRISPR/Cas9 Therapeutics: Recent Advances in Cargo Loading and Targeted Delivery.

abstract: Targeted reduction of hepatic antithrombin (AT) via siRNA offers a promising strategy to enhance thrombin (TMB) generation in bleeding disorders, though efficient hepatocyte delivery remains challenging. This study developed and evaluated a targeted lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation incorporating a novel morpholine-based ionizable lipid (MIL) and a lactobionic-octadecylamine conjugate (LBN) for hepatocyte-specific delivery of AT-siRNA (siAT). Following synthesis of MIL and LBN, siAT-loaded LNP (siAT LNP LBN) were prepared using microfluidics and characterized for size, morphology, zeta potential, polydispersity index, and encapsulation efficiency (EE). Functional assays on HepG2 cells assessed cellular uptake, protein knockdown, and AT activity. The optimized formulation exhibited uniform particles (124 nm, PDI 0.125, zeta potential - 8.9 mV) and high EE (90%). Cytotoxicity assays confirmed safety up to 65 pmol siRNA. LBN-decorated LNP significantly enhanced hepatocyte uptake compared to non-targeted LNP and naked siRNA. Optimal AT mRNA suppression occurred at ~ 65 pmol siRNA and 16 h, with protein knockdown confirmed at 48 h. Functionally, siAT LNP LBN reduced AT activity to 48.1 ± 5.5%, substantially outperforming non-targeted LNP (64.1%) and naked siRNA (86.6%). The developed siAT-LNP-LBN platform demonstrated efficient hepatocyte uptake, robust AT knockdown, and low cytotoxicity in vitro, providing preliminary evidence for its potential as a hepatocyte-targeted siRNA delivery platform. Further in vivo studies are warranted to evaluate its biodistribution, liver-targeting efficiency, pharmacodynamic effects, therapeutic efficacy, and biosafety.

abstract: Delivery formulations that facilitate mRNA transfection in the respiratory system aim to provide a flexible platform to address or prevent respiratory disease in a patient-accessible, targeted manner. Recent clinical trials in cystic fibrosis, respiratory oncology, and mucosal vaccination have exposed the unique physicochemical and immunological challenges that differentiate respiratory and parenteral mRNA strategies. This review examines the nanomaterials, barriers, and experimental models central to the rational development of aerosolized mRNA medicines. We begin with an overview of the most promising classes of devices and nanomaterial formulations used for respiratory delivery. We then analyze the physical barriers to nasal and lung delivery, spanning delivery-associated physical stresses and anatomical matrices, and present the major chemical and biological strategies developed to overcome them. A parallel analysis addresses the immunological barriers of the respiratory mucosa, including the innate and adaptive cell populations and the sensing pathways that mRNA delivery engages. Immunoengineering approaches to improve the tolerability of repeat dosing are discussed, including nucleoside modification and alternative RNA constructs, degradable and anti-inflammatory material chemistries, and co-administration of standard-of-care pulmonary drugs. Finally, we address methodologies for the investigation of the nanomaterial-mucosal interface using biophysical characterization techniques, and evaluate preclinical models spanning in vitro mucus mimics, air-liquid interface cultures, ex vivo precision-cut lung slices, in vivo rodent and non-rodent species, three-dimensional (3D) nasal and lung cast replicas, and mathematical models of the intranasal airways and lung. We propose an interdisciplinary bioengineering approach that combines the expertise of chemists, immunologists, and pulmonologists to enable clinical translation of respiratory mRNA medicines.

abstract: Inherited platelet disorders (IPDs) comprise a heterogeneous group of rare genetic diseases affecting platelet production and/or function, with clinical manifestations ranging from mild mucocutaneous bleeding to severe hemorrhage, multisystem disease, and predisposition to hematologic malignancy. Treatment remains predominantly supportive, and curative options are limited. Future translation will require disease-specific selection of gene addition, allele-specific approaches, or precise genome editing, together with safer conditioning, efficient lineage-restricted correction, and rigorous long-term assessment of genotoxicity and clonal evolution. A shared hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells platform combined with disease-specific genetic engineering may ultimately enable curative treatment of selected severe IPDs.

abstract:
BACKGROUND: Cardiovascular disease (CVD) remains the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in patients with ESKD. Dysregulation of the fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23)/Klotho axis has been implicated in uremic cardiomyopathy, however the mechanism linking dialysis intensity to the regulation of this pathway remains poorly defined.
METHODS: We analyzed serum samples from ESKD patients transitioning from conventional to nocturnal hemodialysis (NHD). Left ventricular mass (LVM) was measured by echocardiography before and after transition. Patients were stratified as LVM regressors [ ≥ 10% decrease in LVM; n = 6] or LVM progressors [ ≥ 10% increase in LVM; n = 7]. Circulating microRNAs (miRs) and serum FGF23 and alpha Klotho were quantified. Mechanistic relevance was tested in an angiotensin-II model of cardiac hypertrophy using FGF23 suppression via an antisense oligonucleotide gapmer, or antagomirs targeting miR-200c-3p.
RESULTS: Among 13 patients transitioning to NHD, LVM regressors required fewer antihypertensive medications than at baseline (P<0.001) with improved metabolic parameters (urea 12.9 vs. 16.6 mmol/L, P<0.01) and higher hemoglobin (109 vs. 95 g/L, P<0.01). We identified six differentially expressed miRs (let-7a/g/i, miR-200c, miR-1 and miR-30c) that targeted the FGF23/Klotho signaling axis. LVM regressors also demonstrated significantly lower circulating FGF23 levels than LVM progressors [60 (28, 160) vs 668 (73, 1734) pg/mL, P<0.05]. In the angiotensin-II murine model of cardiac hypertrophy, FGF23 gapmer treatment or miR-200c-3p inhibition reduced cardiomyocyte hypertrophy and attenuated interstitial fibrosis while restoring FGF23/Klotho signaling through the suppression of extracellular signal-regulated kinase 1/2 phosphorylation, activation of dual specificity phosphatase-1 and inducing antioxidant gene expression.
CONCLUSIONS: Collectively, these exploratory findings link dialysis intensification to miR-mediated regulation of the FGF23/Klotho axis, demonstrating that targeting this regulatory network is sufficient to suppress pathological cardiac remodeling. These data provide a mechanistic basis for the cardiovascular benefits of nocturnal hemodialysis and identify the FGF23/Klotho axis as a candidate therapeutic target warranting further validation.

abstract: Natural killer (NK) cells have emerged as promising candidates for adoptive immunotherapies. Their natural cytotoxic capabilities and low incidence of side-effects such as cytokine release syndrome and immune effector cell-associated neurotoxicity, render NK cells a favorable alternative to T cells. Incorporation of a chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) has been shown to greatly enhance NK cell's antitumor capacity. Nevertheless, CAR-NK cell therapies still face several challenges, such as low in vivo persistence, low tumor homing of the transfused cells and the effects of the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment (TME). Genetic modifications of key cellular mediators show great potential to overcome these hurdles. While well-established viral engineering strategies are currently the most commonly used techniques, biosafety concerns, high costs, and labour-intensive protocols have encouraged innovation toward nonviral strategies. In this review, we describe recently established viral and nonviral technologies used for NK cell engineering, focusing on their respective advantages and disadvantages. In addition, we highlight the most important functional refinements and mechanistic characterizations of NK cells and genetically optimized NK cells in the context of the TME and how these advances can be progressed toward therapeutic translation.

title: Killers by Design: How Innovative Gene-Engineering Fine-Tunes NK Cells as Next Generation Immunotherapies.

abstract: Infectious diseases continue to pose a global health challenge, intensified by antimicrobial resistance and limitations of pharmaceutical countermeasures. Nanotechnology offers a promising front against these barriers using intelligent, multifunctional systems. This review explores the convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI), CRISPR gene editing, bacteriophage therapy, and immune modulation within the framework of second-generation nanoparticle therapeutics. AI-guided modelling enables predictive optimization of nanoparticle design on the basis of size, charge, and surface proteins, targeting specific pathogens and providing enhanced stability. Consequently, nanoparticles serve as precision nanocarriers and protective delivery vehicles for the CRISPR-Cas system, shielding nucleic acid cargo from enzymatic degradation and enabling targeted intracellular delivery via pH-responsive endosomal escape mechanisms. The nanoparticles not only provide protection but also enable tissue-targeting and infection-site-specific delivery of the CRISPR-Cas system, facilitating precise genome editing to reverse resistance in specific pathogens such as HIV and Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Phage nanoparticle hybrids further expand antimicrobial potency by enhancing phage stability, delivery, and host range. Moreover, engineered nanoparticles modulate the immune system via immunosuppressive and immunostimulant strategies for reducing hyperinflammation and enhancing pathogen clearance, respectively. Despite such encouraging laboratory outcomes, the clinical translation of AI-integrated nanoparticle platforms still faces a number of obstacles. Large-scale manufacturing, scalability, and reproducibility pose a significant challenge. Regulatory approvals for such multi-modal nano-drugs seem to get bogged down due to vague and scarce exemplary proofs. Furthermore, safety and efficacy apprehensions, unpredictable and complex host-phage interactions, cost-effectiveness, and equitable access remain a subject matter of concern. Conclusively, the convergence of advanced nanotechnology, artificial intelligence, and synthetic biology marks the dawn of a transformative era in infectious disease therapeutics where treatment is not only intelligent and adaptive but also ethically and globally inclusive.Clinical trial registrationNot applicable.

abstract: CRISPR-Cas9 has transformed agricultural biotechnology, microbial engineering, and human therapeutics within a decade, yet biosafety assessment remains focused on editing accuracy and off-target cleavage. A second, neglected question is what the high-molecular-weight Cas9 effector protein does to expressing systems. This review integrates evidence from eukaryotic cell lines, microbial hosts, transgenic mammals, and dietary exposure models. In isolated cells Cas9 injures the host by three routes, only one requiring DNA cleavage: TP53-dependent genotoxic stress at susceptible loci, modified by cell sex and p53 status; guide-independent binding to ribosomal proteins that activates the PI3K-mTORC2 axis; and promiscuous association with host transcripts inducing a p53-linked stress programme. In GC-rich bacteria, PAM density and limited double-strand break repair make basal expression lethal. Intact mammals tolerate tissue-restricted Cas9 expression, although nervous system and germline compartments are exceptions, and dietary exposure carries no measurable toxicological or allergenic risk. Pre-existing anti-Cas9 immunity is the dominant translational barrier. Proteasomal, SUMO-regulated and autophagic pathways together set Cas9 half-life. Transient ribonucleoprotein delivery, anti-CRISPR, degron-based control, and lower-toxicity orthogonal nucleases each narrow this exposure window. We conclude that Cas9 toxicity is not intrinsic but contingent on expression kinetics, delivery format, host repair, proteostatic capacity, and immunological history. Biosafety is therefore a tunable design parameter, and this review provides a mechanism-based framework for matching nuclease, delivery route and temporal control to the intended application.

title: DDX5 mRNA-targeting antisense oligonucleotide as a new promising therapeutic in combating castration-resistant prostate cancer.

abstract: Nucleic acid therapeutics have transformed modern medicine, enabling targeted treatments that address a wide range of diseases at their genetic roots. From RNAi-mediated gene silencing to mRNA vaccines and CRISPR-based editing, these advances offer precision strategies for previously intractable conditions. The success of these modalities hinges entirely on delivery technologies which have evolved lockstep with nucleic acid research, facilitating transport from administration site to intracellular target(s). Lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) have emerged as the leading delivery platform for nucleic acid therapeutics which is partially due to extensive research and development of lipid-based vehicle derivatives previously developed for small molecule-based drugs. While LNPs themselves have a relatively brief clinical history, the COVID-19 pandemic propelled nucleic acid technologies into the global spotlight, accelerating public, industrial, and regulatory engagement. This surge in attention catalyzed the maturation of clinical, manufacturing, and regulatory frameworks for therapies that rely on delivery technologies like LNPs for success. While this progress has enabled a new wave of therapies, it has also underscored the limitations of LNPs, including poor penetration into dense extracellular matrix (ECM) tissues and dose-limiting toxicities driven by immunogenicity. As optimization of LNP formulations continues, a new generation of nanoparticle platforms is emerging, aiming to address these shortcomings in morphology, chemistry, and tissue specificity. These platforms are well-positioned to leverage the translational groundwork laid by LNPs, potentially accelerating their own path to clinical relevance. In this review, we examine the evolution and clinical impact of LNPs, analyze their key limitations, and explore emerging delivery platforms, such as biomimetic nanoparticles and polymeric systems that seek to overcome the physicochemical limitations of LNPs while building on the lessons and regulatory frameworks they established.

title: Lipid nanoparticles and their successors: Design principles for dense tissue penetration and clinical translation.

abstract: The composition of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) strongly affects the nucleic acid loading, the interactions with biological targets, the effective endosomal escape, and the cytosolic release at the target site. To integrate these requirements and evaluate the effect of excipients commonly used in LNP production, we comparatively screened a set of LNP formulations containing nucleic acid condensing tetraArginine-[G2]-distearoyl glycerol (OCE), and different fusogenic/ionizable commercial lipids: DOPE, DODAP, D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102. Three PEGylated agents were investigated to evaluate their effect on colloidal stability and transfection performance: pH-sheddable DSPE-hydrazone-PEG2kDa (DSPE-Hz-PEG), diffusible DMG-PEG2kDa (DMG-PEG) and non-releasable DSPE-PEG2kDa (NR-DSPE-PEG). The combination of OCE with the commercial lipids yielded LNPs with ~100 nm sizes, and + 35/40 mV z-potentials, and high siRNA loading efficiencies (~90%), nearly doubling those of OCE-free formulations. LNPs containing OCE and the ionizable lipids D-Lin-MC3-DMA, ALC-0315, and SM-102 yielded the highest gene silencing in eGFP-expressing H1299 cells, with IC₅₀ values between 0.32 and 0.47 nM. In contrast, all OCE-free formulations and formulations containing OCE in combination with DOPE or DODAP, yielded remarkably lower gene silencing. LNPs obtained with OCE and SM-102 coated with 3 and 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG and NR-DSPE-PEG produced colloidally stable formulations also in presence of serum. The 5 mol% DSPE-Hz-PEG coating provided effective charge shielding at pH 7.4 while PEG detached under endosomal conditions (pH 5.5). This behavior enhanced cytosolic siRNA delivery, achieving an eGFP silencing IC₅₀ of 3.22 nM owing to efficient OCE-LNP endosomal escape enabled by spatially controlled, pH-triggered cleavage of the PEG-lipid. NR-DSPE-PEG showed reduced endosomal escape and transfection (IC₅₀: 82 nM) while DMG-PEG exhibited poor serum stability due to premature detachment, making it a less effective stealth agent.

abstract: Previously, we used an aminooxy click chemistry (AOCC) strategy to introduce pairs of ligands into oligonucleotides during solid-phase synthesis by using nucleoside and non-nucleoside building blocks. However, the standard oligonucleotide synthesis conditions were incompatible with the incorporation of certain complex ligands. In this report, first, a post-oligonucleotide synthesis solution-phase AOCC approach was developed to address this issue. Different pairs of ligands were conjugated to oligonucleotides through an O-amino building block incorporated during the solid-phase synthesis. Second, a small interfering RNA with a sense strand conjugated using the AOCC strategy to target the ApoB gene using a receptor-targeting ligand (GalNAc) and a pharmacokinetic enhancer (C16 alkyl) was evaluated in mice. The bis-heteroconjugate had a longer duration of action and higher level of silencing than the siRNA carrying only the receptor-targeting ligand.

abstract: Antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) lipid nanoparticles (LNPs) remain underexplored relative to siRNA and mRNA LNPs. Using an orthogonal workflow (DLS, NTA, AF4), we show that ionisable lipid identity and microfluidic flow rate govern key LNP attributes. Replacing SM-102 with MC3 increased size and reduced ASO recovery, while lower flow rates increased LNP size and improved recovery, highlighting formulation-property relationships for ASO LNP optimisation.
